```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(evca)
```

# The claim

Decision analysis in the tradition of Howard and Keeney aims to give the
parties one decision model: shared variables, a shared causal structure and one
value function [@howard1968; @keeney1976; @keeney1992; @howard2015]. The
decision quality chain (frame, alternatives, information, values, logic,
commitment) is the discipline for getting there.

Some decision professionals hold that when stakeholders' causal models and
value variables do not overlap, the framing has failed: with better framing and
pre-framing the ontologies merge. This vignette argues for a narrower claim.

> Careful framing removes **linguistic** and **evidential** disagreement. It
> need not remove **ontological-evaluative** disagreement: accounts that carry
> different causal structures and different things of value. No observation
> settles that disagreement, because the accounts do not share the variable
> that an observation would measure. Each account can still be tested on its
> own terms, and parts of one account can be criticised from another. Groups
> still have to act together in that case.

The distinction is between two senses of "ambiguity". In standard decision
analysis, ambiguity and uncertainty are epistemic: a missing probability or an
unclear statement that more probing could resolve. The ontological-evaluative
kind is not that. More probing sharpens each account but does not merge them.

`evca` prices this situation. It does not resolve it. Everything below uses
constructed numbers; no result is an empirical finding.

# Three kinds of ambiguity

| Kind | Typical symptom | What reduces it |
|---|---|---|
| Linguistic / framing | Same word, different variable | Clarity test, better framing [@howard2015] |
| Evidential | Disputed effect size or state | Data, elicitation, value of information |
| Ontological-evaluative | Different causal structure and different valued outcomes | Not more data on a shared variable. Option design, rules, side payments, governance |

The weights in `evca` mark the same split [@strong2012; @bojke2009]. With
**epistemic** probabilities over models the shortfall is the expected value of
perfect information about the model index, so evidence can reduce it. With
**evaluative** weights it is an aggregation shortfall. It is the price of
choosing one action for accounts that rank actions differently, and research does
not remove it.

# A running example

Three accounts rate three road options. The numbers are illustrative.

```{r example}
U_raw <- matrix(
  c( 5, 40, 80,
    90, 82,  8,
    72, 78, 55),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    c("No road", "Direct route", "Rerouted road"),
    c("Officials", "ProDev_Hmong", "Traditional_Hmong")
  )
)
w <- rep(1/3, 3)  # declared standing, not probabilities
U <- normalize_utilities(U_raw)
compute_evca(U, model_weights = w)$evca
```

Before any scale choice, ask whether the accounts agree on the best action at
all. This uses only each account's own ranking.

```{r agreement}
check_action_agreement(U_raw)$agree
```

If the accounts agreed, EVCA would be zero for every weighting and rescaling.
They do not, so it is positive for every positive weighting and rescaling. This
conclusion does not depend on the contested common scale.

# The reframing test

The objection is that a positive EVCA only shows poor framing. This can be
tested. Have independent facilitators reframe the problem and compute EVCA for
each framing. If EVCA falls to zero under some defensible framing, the
disagreement was framing. If it stays materially above zero across framings,
the residual is consistent with ontological-evaluative disagreement. It does not prove it, because other framings may exist that no one has tried.

Below, framing 2 adds a co-managed option, a typical product of better
alternative generation. Framing 3 adds a clarity-test revision: officials and
the pro-development account were using "development" for different variables,
and the revision moves one column.

```{r reframing}
framings <- list(
  "F1 original" = U_raw,
  "F2 + co-managed option" = rbind(
    U_raw, "Co-managed road" = c(60, 70, 70)
  ),
  "F3 + clarified 'development'" = {
    m <- rbind(U_raw, "Co-managed road" = c(60, 70, 70))
    m[, "ProDev_Hmong"] <- c(20, 85, 80, 78)
    m
  }
)

reframe_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(framings), function(f) {
  Uf <- normalize_utilities(framings[[f]])
  r <- compute_evca(Uf, model_weights = w)
  data.frame(framing = f, evca = round(r$evca, 3),
             shared_action = rownames(Uf)[r$optimal_decision],
             accounts_agree = check_action_agreement(framings[[f]])$agree)
}))
reframe_table
```

Adding an option leaves EVCA unchanged here and the clarity revision lowers it
only slightly, so most of it is residual. The framing-reducible part is the drop
from F1 to the best framing and the residual is what remains. This
suggests a reportable quantity, a **value of reframing**: the original EVCA
minus the smallest EVCA across independent defensible framings. The residual
needs governance rather than research. The package does not implement this as a
function. The test is only as strong as the independence of the facilitators
and the defensibility of the framings.

# The scale is part of the dispute

EVCA is a scalar and needs a bridge that puts accounts on one scale. In the
incommensurable case that bridge is exactly what is contested
[@macaskill2016; @chang1997]. Report the result under several bridges and flag
when the recommended action flips.

```{r bridges}
bridge_minmax <- function(M) normalize_utilities(M)
bridge_z <- function(M) apply(M, 2, function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x))
bridge_rank <- function(M) apply(M, 2, function(x) (rank(x) - 1) / (length(x) - 1))
bridge_raw <- function(M) M / 100  # treats the 0-100 ratings as comparable

bridges <- list(`min-max` = bridge_minmax, `z-score` = bridge_z,
                `rank` = bridge_rank, `raw` = bridge_raw)

bridge_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(bridges), function(b) {
  Ub <- bridges[[b]](framings[[2]])
  r <- compute_evca(Ub, model_weights = w)
  data.frame(bridge = b, evca = round(r$evca, 3),
             shared_action = rownames(Ub)[r$optimal_decision])
}))
bridge_table
```

EVCA values on different bridges are not comparable with each other, only the
direction and the shared action are. A shared action that changes with the
bridge is a finding in itself.

# A version that needs no common scale

If cardinal comparability is the thing in dispute, drop it. Each account states
what it can accept, for example "within 25 points of my best". The question
then is whether a jointly acceptable action exists. This follows the logic of
overlapping consensus and incompletely theorized agreement, in which parties
accept the same action for different reasons [@rawls1987; @sunstein1995].

```{r acceptable}
acceptable <- function(M, tol) {
  best <- apply(M, 2, max)
  ok <- sweep(M, 2, best - tol, ">=")
  rownames(M)[rowSums(ok) == ncol(M)]
}
acceptable(framings[[2]], tol = 25)
acceptable(framings[[2]], tol = 10)
```

Tolerances are each account's own. An empty set at tolerances the accounts
regard as legitimate is a genuine conflict. A non-empty set gives an action
everyone can live with, without claiming that their utilities are comparable.
The tolerance is a declared acceptability threshold and is not elicited by
`evca`.

# Option design: the "reverse game theory" move

Mechanism design chooses the game to get a desired outcome. The analogue here
is to choose the option set and the contract to shrink the shortfall. Exclusion
costs show who bears the loss.

```{r exclusion}
Uf <- normalize_utilities(framings[[2]])
compute_exclusion_costs(Uf, model_weights = w, normalize = FALSE)
```

Searching over candidate packages is straightforward: compute EVCA for each
candidate option set and keep the one with the smallest shortfall that every
account can accept. Two cautions apply. Standard mechanism design assumes a
common outcome space, which is the thing missing here. Closer formal homes are
games with unawareness, where players do not represent the same game
[@heifetz2006], and bargaining solutions that measure distance from each
party's ideal point [@kalai1975]. EVCA is a diagnostic of that distance and
not a solution concept. Accounts that inflate their stakes to enlarge their
share of the shortfall are a further strategic concern that EVCA does not
address.

# Joint ventures

Joint venture partners typically hold different causal theories (market,
regulation, technology, community response) and different objectives (return,
learning, control, reputation, social licence) [@kogut1988; @parkhe1993].
Three features of `evca` map onto this.

* **Exclusion cost** is a partner's loss if the decision is made without its
  account, a walk-away measure.
* **Dirichlet sensitivity** shows how robust the shared action is to disputes
  over standing, such as equity share or governance rights.
* **Transferability** decides how much of the shortfall can be bought out
  [@coase1960; @grossman1986].

```{r jv}
jv <- matrix(
  c(10, 12,
    18,  2,
     8, 11),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("Expand", "License out", "Joint plant"),
                  c("Partner_A", "Partner_B"))
)
w_jv <- c(0.5, 0.5)
disagreement <- c(Partner_A = 6, Partner_B = 5)  # payoff if the JV dissolves

# Non-transferable payoffs: only the action matters.
nt <- compute_evca(normalize_utilities(jv), model_weights = w_jv)
list(evca_non_transferable = nt$evca,
     shared_action = rownames(jv)[nt$optimal_decision])

# Transferable (cash) payoffs: pick the largest total, then check whether a
# side payment leaves both partners above their disagreement payoff.
total <- rowSums(jv)
best <- which.max(total)
surplus_over_exit <- total[best] - sum(disagreement)
list(action = rownames(jv)[best], total = unname(total[best]),
     surplus_over_exit = unname(surplus_over_exit))
```

With transferable payoffs, a positive surplus over the exit payoffs means a
transfer can leave both partners better off than dissolving, so most of the
shortfall can be bargained away. With non-transferable outcomes such as control
rights, reputation or community effects, it cannot, and EVCA remains the cost
of acting together.

Partners with different priors may also use contingent contracts, such as
earn-outs and staged commitments, which let each side expect to gain on its own
beliefs. This works because agreeing to disagree needs a common prior
[@aumann1976].

# Two layers of weights

Keep two kinds of weights apart. Within an account, uncertainty about states is
ordinary Bayesian and is reduced by evidence. Across accounts, weights are
evaluative standing. `evca_decompose()` separates the two parts of the gap.

```{r decompose}
set.seed(1)
mu <- U_raw
draws <- array(NA_real_, c(500, 3, 3))
for (i in 1:500) draws[i, , ] <- mu + rnorm(9, sd = 6)
evca_decompose(draws, model_weights = w,
               scale_min = apply(mu, 2, min),
               scale_range = apply(mu, 2, function(x) diff(range(x))))
```

`evpi_agg` is ordinary EVPI about the state and can be reduced by evidence.
`evca_post` is the shortfall that remains when the state is known. Applying
Bayesian model averaging across accounts [@hoeting1999] would silently turn
standing into belief; it is legitimate only within the first layer. All
accounts must be expressed over the same states. Where some accounts contain
states others cannot represent, the union of states with "not applicable"
cells is a workaround, not a solution.

# Position in the literature

* **Structural uncertainty.** Model uncertainty and averaging
  [@draper1995; @madigan1994; @hoeting1999] assume the model set contains
  something useful and that weights are beliefs. When no model is true and none
  is in the set (the M-open case, [@bernardo1994]), stacking and generalized
  Bayes [@yao2018; @bissiri2016] and robust decisions under approximate models
  [@watson2016] apply. Health economics has the nearest value-of-information
  work on structural uncertainty [@bojke2009; @strong2012]. `evca` adds a
  separate reading of the weights for accounts that are not rival guesses about
  one world.
* **Ambiguity and robustness.** Maxmin, smooth ambiguity, robust control and
  scenario-based methods [@ellsberg1961; @gilboa1989; @klibanoff2005;
  @hansen2001; @lempert2003] model one agent with non-unique beliefs. The case
  here has several agents with non-unique worlds and values.
* **Group beliefs and tastes.** Pooling and aggregation results
  [@harsanyi1955; @genest1986; @nau2002] come with a warning. Agreement on an
  action cannot generally be combined with Bayesian aggregation when beliefs
  differ [@seidenfeld1989; @mongin1995; @gilboa2004]. A shared choice can hide
  disagreement about why, and EVCA exposes the cost of that hiding.
* **Incommensurability and agreement across it.** Overlapping consensus,
  incompletely theorized agreement, boundary objects and trading zones all
  describe action without shared reasons
  [@rawls1987; @sunstein1995; @star1989; @galison1997], and post-normal science
  and opening-up appraisal argue for plural framings
  [@funtowicz1993; @stirling2010].
* **Decision analysis.** Practitioners have long aimed at a requisite model,
  sufficient to act on rather than complete [@phillips1984]. The claim here is
  that requisite for a group may mean requisite plural.

# Objections and limits

* **"Good framing makes EVCA zero."** The reframing test is the answer. A
  positive finding across independent framings is evidence for the residual. A
  zero under a defensible framing is evidence against it. Both outcomes are
  informative.
* **"Equal weights are neutral."** They are a choice. Who sets the weights
  matters at least as much as their values, and Dirichlet sensitivity explores
  alternatives but does not legitimize any of them.
* **"The scalar needs a common scale."** Yes. Use the bridge sensitivity and the
  acceptability analysis above, and report which conclusions survive.
* **Outside the package.** `evca` does not build the causal models, elicit the
  utilities or justify a bridge. It takes finished account-level payoffs and
  reports what choosing one action costs each account.

# Reporting checklist

1. What each account is, and who selected the accounts.
2. Who chose the weights, what they represent, and results under alternatives.
3. The bridge, and the actions that flip under other bridges.
4. EVCA across independent framings, and the residual.
5. Exclusion costs per account.
6. Whether payoffs are transferable.
7. The acceptability analysis, if no scale is agreed.
